subtitle: When someone introduces themselves, this course helps you receive the name they offer and understand what it means in that moment. You will also learn to keep introductions separate from official records and from assumptions about identity.
scope: For staff across DHS. Original adult cases examine names, personally learned meaning, practical introductions and respectful correction. They do not assign nationality, kinship, gender, language ability or an individual IDI orientation from a name. General international web-design guidance does not authorize changing actual agency forms or records. Actual equity, information and protected-class responsibilities retain their appropriate scope and roles. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA. Participation in this learning is voluntary.
introTranscript: Mara Ellis asks to be introduced by both words of her name. Jo offers a chosen short name. Hear their different experiences of recognition and welcome, reconsider an initial judgment about formality and choose a fitting response without requiring family history or public cultural proof. The full example or private unrecorded reflection is enough.

intro.heading: Hear a name without turning it into a profile
intro.body:
In this original practice learning case, two adults are considering an optional neighborhood reading evening. Mara Ellis asks to be introduced using both words, “Mara Ellis.” Jo says, “Please call me Jo in the discussion.” Ada, who is preparing a possible introduction, initially treats Mara as unnecessarily formal and Jo as insufficiently serious. No country, legal name, family relationship, gender identity, language proficiency or actual event approval is supplied. The names and requests are what the learner knows.

W3C’s internationalization article, Personal names around the world, introduces variation in names and its implications for web forms. It cautions against assuming a universal order, number of parts or preferred form of address, and relates design choices to the application’s purpose. It is general practical guidance, not a complete account of every person or a rule governing Minnesota records. Its country examples should not become a script applied to an individual merely because a name looks familiar.

The purpose distinction helps Ada. A spoken introduction, a contribution label and an official identity record need not ask the same question. Mara’s request identifies how she wants to be introduced in this encounter. Jo’s request identifies a form of address for discussion. Neither tells Ada what belongs in an official record, permits a public biographical account or supplies qualification for an agency role. An unfamiliar arrangement is a reason to receive the person’s explanation, not to invent a missing name part or demand a more familiar substitute.

Ada can recognize that her judgments go beyond the requests. Formality may have a meaningful reason other than distance; a short name may have a reason other than carelessness. The next lessons provide Mara’s and Jo’s accounts rather than ask the learner to guess them. A useful first step is to keep the offered name, the intended use and the missing information distinct.

Privately explain one assumption Ada has added. You may reflect unrecorded on a name or form of address that matters to you, or use only the full example. No family history, public introduction or live form revision is required. Understanding how you learned a naming expectation can be meaningful even before any workplace application.

items.title: Keep the supplied request intact
items.body: Mara asks for both words in the introduction; Jo offers Jo for discussion. Replacing either request with Ada’s preferred format would answer a different question. The case does not tell the learner whether either name matches a formal record, so that issue should remain open rather than be solved by guessing.

items.title: Notice the assumption behind the judgment
items.body: Ada treats a full introduction as distance and a short name as lack of seriousness. These are interpretations, not facts supplied by the names. Recognizing the interpretation creates room to hear an individual reason without demanding proof that a chosen name deserves respect.

items.title: Use general guidance for its purpose
items.body: W3C explains that forms can make mistaken assumptions about name parts and address. It does not provide a universal perfect layout or permission to change an actual database. Its practical question is what the particular use needs, which Ada can ask without making a country-based rule.

tabs.label: A familiar template decides every name
tabs.body: Ada divides every name into two expected positions and adds a missing family name to Jo. The supplied request does not authorize that invention. A familiar template may be convenient for Ada while misrepresenting the person; the intended use and actual requirements need examination.

tabs.label: The name supplies a whole identity
tabs.body: Ada assigns nationality, ability and family history from how the names look. The example describes none of those details. Even a general article’s examples cannot turn resemblance into an individual identity or an explanation of this person’s preference.

tabs.label: The request and purpose guide the next question
tabs.body: Ada receives the names and considers their proposed use in an introduction. Where another purpose actually arises, she can ask the relevant question through its appropriate arrangements. This preserves an individual request without treating it as a complete record or capability profile.

intro.heading: Separate an introduction from a record requirement
intro.body:
Ada drafts two questions for the possible reading evening: “What name would you like in the introduction?” and “What should we call you in discussion?” The questions concern participation in this optional personal encounter. They are not an actual DHS intake form, a record-correction request or a new agency requirement. Mara’s and Jo’s offered answers can guide the stated use without requiring legal documents or a complete history.

The distinction is practical. A name on an introduction can identify the chosen contribution, while a spoken form of address can help the discussion. W3C’s general guidance suggests considering why separate name parts are needed and whether asking for a form of address would avoid assumptions. It does not mean that every real form must use Ada’s two questions or that every official purpose can be handled by a single unrestricted text field. Actual record and system requirements retain their own authority and process.

Ada considers adding “Explain where your name comes from” as a required question. That would change the purpose. Neither the introduction nor a respectful discussion requires the course learner to establish a family story. A person may choose to offer meaning later, but a clear naming request can stand without that disclosure. The learner should not equate a declined story with an invalid name, unwillingness to participate or an unsuccessful cultural identity.

Ada also considers publishing the introduction list online. The example describes neither an approved event nor permission for that public use. Asking about a spoken introduction does not by itself establish permission for a website, a recording or an official data change. Ada needs to keep those different questions visible rather than treat one answer as consent to every possible use. The course does not determine any real information classification or release decision.

A fitting proposal would explain the particular use and invite a relevant answer. If the actual issue involved an official record, staff would follow its appropriate requirements and assigned roles rather than improvise a correction. In this complete fiction, the proposed questions are enough to practice receiving information at its stated scope. Privately compare them with the added biography and publication assumptions; no actual form must be built or changed.

items.title: Use two questions for two reasons
items.body: Ada’s draft separates a chosen introduction from a discussion address. The difference helps avoid automatically extracting one part of a name for every greeting. Mara may offer the same wording for both purposes or different wording; the course does not supply a new answer simply because two fields are proposed.

items.title: Avoid a story as the price of accuracy
items.body: A family-history question can be an optional conversation when welcome, but it is not needed to receive the current requests. Making it compulsory shifts the purpose from naming to cultural disclosure. A person can keep the story private while still offering the name that fits this encounter.

items.title: Retain another use as another question
items.body: Posting the list online would be a different use from a spoken introduction. The proposed answer does not establish that permission or an official record correction. If an actual task requires additional information, use its real arrangements rather than treat this voluntary draft as a universal process.

tabs.label: Collect everything for a simple introduction
tabs.body: Ada requires legal records, family history and nationality before accepting a name for discussion. The complete personal case supplies no purpose for that collection. More information is not automatically more respectful, and it can turn a chosen contribution into an unnecessary disclosure test.

tabs.label: One answer authorizes every use
tabs.body: Ada treats the introduction name as permission for a website, a recording and official database changes. Those uses have different questions and requirements. The supplied request may guide the introduction while public use and formal changes remain unconfirmed.

tabs.label: Explain the use and retain its limits
tabs.body: Ada asks for the introduction name and discussion address with their purpose made clear. She leaves publication and formal record matters with their own requirements. This keeps the proposed questions useful without requiring a story or making a new agency procedure.

check.question: What is the value of Ada’s two proposed questions?
check.correct: They make introduction and discussion purposes clearer without establishing legal-record status, public-use permission or a mandatory biography.
wrong: They prove that every agency form must adopt these exact two fields.
They require nationality and family history before a naming request counts.
They authorize all future publication and official corrections.
check.feedbackCorrect: The proposal serves the particular encounter while leaving different uses and actual requirements separate.
check.feedbackIncorrect: General design advice is not an exact mandatory DHS form. A biography does not validate the offered name. An introduction answer is not blanket permission for publication or formal correction; those matters retain their own arrangements.

takeaways: A naming preference can carry a learned relationship to recognition.

lessons.statement: Let the offered meaning change the judgment and the response.

image.caption: Five people sit around a white table with notebooks and laptops; whiteboards are visible beside them.

intro.heading: Understand what recognition and familiarity mean
intro.body:
Mara chooses to explain why she wants both words in the introduction. In her family’s handwritten recipe cards, a contributor’s full offered name accompanied the dish so that repeated sharing did not make its creator disappear. She learned that naming a contribution accurately could express care for the person who made it. Mara is not claiming that every family uses this practice or asking Ada to investigate her genealogy. She offers a particular meaning that connects her request to recognition.

Jo chooses a different account. In a local stage crew, people asked what they should call one another before working together. Jo chose Jo and learned that receiving a chosen short address could invite someone into the shared effort without deciding their status. The short form became meaningful because it was offered and received, not because shortening every name is automatically friendly. Jo is not asking Ada to shorten Mara’s name or claiming that a nickname proves every person feels welcome.

These accounts widen Ada’s initial judgments. Mara’s full introduction can retain a contribution rather than create distance. Jo’s short address can retain a chosen relationship rather than signal lack of seriousness. Both can be received without ranking one as the more authentic, mature or culturally important form. The Council of Europe’s discussion of personalized cultural affiliations supports learning from such individual meanings, while preserving variation within groups.

Ada proposes introducing Mara as Mara Ellis and addressing Jo as Jo in the discussion, subject to checking the intended use with them. She can also invite another preference if the context differs. The response changes because she understands recognition and chosen familiarity, not merely because she remembers to fill a field. Neither a final introduction nor accepted public use is supplied yet.

An optional private reflection can examine how you learned a naming expectation: through family, friendship, a chosen activity, a place or an experience of being addressed. You can understand that connection without disclosing a name history, staging a conversation or proving a workplace improvement. The complete Mara and Jo fiction is an equally valid path. Their accounts provide enough meaning to practice widening an interpretation and proposing a different response.

items.title: Mara’s full name is about a contribution
items.body: The recipe-card practice connects an accurately named maker with repeated sharing. Ada’s distance label overlooks that learned relationship. Hearing the meaning helps Ada receive both words without demanding that Mara prove formal status or publish the family story.

items.title: Jo’s short name is about a chosen welcome
items.body: The stage-crew practice made asking and receiving the chosen address important. Ada’s seriousness label overlooks that willingness. The lesson is not that every nickname is friendly; the chosen form has a meaning here, and Mara’s different request remains equally possible.

items.title: The changed response follows the meanings
items.body: Ada proposes a full introduction for Mara and Jo for discussion rather than forcing one format on both. She can explain the contribution and choice reasons without claiming acceptance or a lasting cultural trait. Private understanding can retain this wider view even if the evening never occurs.

tabs.label: One form is inherently more respectful
tabs.body: Ada ranks full names as mature and short names as careless. Jo’s chosen account shows why that ranking misses a particular experience; Mara’s account also does not require the same form for every person. Respect depends on receiving the request and its context rather than a universal hierarchy of length.

tabs.label: A meaningful account requires public biography
tabs.body: Ada accepts the requests only if both adults let her retell their histories in the introduction. Explaining a meaning does not grant public-story permission. She can use the offered name without making the person a compulsory cultural example.

tabs.label: Different meanings inform particular responses
tabs.body: Ada receives contribution recognition and chosen familiarity, then changes the proposed introduction and discussion address. The account remains individual rather than a family or crew-wide prediction. A different answer and private reflection are still possible, so understanding does not become a fixed profile.

check.feedbackIncorrect: One person’s account is not every relative’s rule. Jo’s chosen short form does not authorize an unchosen nickname for Mara or anyone else. Offered meaning is not public-story permission; Ada can receive the name without retelling the history.

lessons.statement: Receive the correction, clarify what is needed and return to the contribution.

image.caption: Five people sit around a white table with notebooks and laptops; whiteboards are visible beside them.

intro.heading: Receive a correction and clarify pronunciation respectfully
intro.body:
Now consider this particular exchange. Ada drafts an introduction using “Mara,” and Mara responds, “Please use Mara Ellis when you introduce my contribution.” Ada has a clear written correction. She does not yet have an audio example, a phonetic explanation, permission to make a recording or a new preference for every setting. The course does not simulate an actual pronunciation or ask the learner to guess one from letters.

A fitting reply could be, “Thank you for the correction. I will use Mara Ellis in the introduction. Is there anything about how I say it that you would like me to check?” This receives the specific request and leaves a relevant answer possible. Mara can offer pronunciation guidance, confirm no further clarification is needed or choose another response. The proposed question is not a requirement that Mara explain her ancestry, provide unlimited coaching or perform publicly for Ada. No answer to it is supplied.

W3C’s name article notes that written forms and pronunciation can have ambiguity and that expectations about address vary. The practical lesson is to avoid treating spelling, apparent origin or a familiar name pattern as automatic knowledge. It does not require a recording of every colleague or provide a universal phonetic method. Actual accessibility, information and workplace arrangements still matter if a real task arises.

Ada considers making a long public explanation of how hard unfamiliar names are for her. That would turn Mara’s specific correction into responsibility for Ada’s comfort and put the person back in the spotlight. A proportionate acknowledgment can retain the contribution and change the next use. It need not demand forgiveness or insist that the person certify Ada’s intent. Likewise, treating one mistake as proof of a permanent identity or policy finding would exceed this supplied exchange; actual concerns retain their appropriate process.

Privately choose the next sentence and describe what remains unanswered. You can use the full example without recording your own name or another person’s voice. Practicing a respectful correction can be meaningful learning even when the actual pronunciation remains unknown.

items.title: Receive the requested change

items.title: Ask about pronunciation without creating a performance
items.body: Ada can invite relevant guidance while allowing a chosen answer. The written form is not an audio demonstration, and a general name pattern is not this person’s pronunciation. The course neither requires a recording nor approves collection or sharing of one.

items.title: Keep acknowledgment proportionate
items.body: A brief acknowledgment and changed action can receive the correction without asking Mara to comfort Ada or explain a full history. The response is still a proposal until used. A person need not accept an apology or reassure the speaker for their naming request to be considered.

tabs.label: Intent replaces the correction
tabs.body: Ada says she meant to be friendly, so Mara must accept the shorter introduction. Intent does not answer the supplied request. Keeping the current use would preserve Ada’s interpretation instead of the requested form and leave the contribution misnamed in the draft.

tabs.label: The correction becomes a public lesson about the person
tabs.body: Ada asks Mara to tell the whole room about family history and repeatedly demonstrate pronunciation. The correction does not authorize that public role or unlimited instruction. A relevant optional question can clarify what is needed without turning the contributor into a compulsory source of personal information.

tabs.label: A brief acknowledgment changes the proposed use
tabs.body: Ada receives Mara Ellis for the introduction and invites only a relevant pronunciation clarification. She retains the unanswered part and returns to the contribution. This is a practical repair proposal rather than proof of forgiveness, a completed event or universal future preference.

wrong: Insist friendly intent makes the unwanted shortened introduction correct.

check.feedbackCorrect: This receives the concrete request while keeping unknown pronunciation and unrelated uses separate.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Friendly intent does not erase the request for both words. A history or public lesson is not needed to receive that correction. The written form does not supply pronunciation, record authority or every future preference; those are different questions.

lessons.statement: Receive a concern without making optional learning a gate to an actual duty.

image.caption: Five people sit around a white table with notebooks and laptops; whiteboards are visible beside them.

intro.heading: Keep a naming concern with its actual responsibilities
intro.body:
A separate original workplace example gives the manager a specific role. Supervisor Casey receives an allegation that a colleague deliberately shortens another employee’s name in connection with that employee’s national origin. No investigation finding is supplied. This allegation is distinct from Mara’s personal reading-evening correction; the course does not turn every mistake or preferred name into an established policy violation.

Current MMB Policy 1436 includes repeatedly or deliberately mispronouncing a person’s name related to protected class, including an unwelcome nickname or shortening without permission, among its conduct examples. The actual relationship and context matter for a finding. That distinction does not create a proof threshold before Casey’s supervisor report. Managers and supervisors immediately report all protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and comply with their agency’s complaint and investigation procedures and/or Affirmative Action Plan.

Casey cannot delay for a pronunciation test, a family story, an accepted apology, the course’s terminology, a consultant response or agreement that every naming preference is cultural. The required report is not a finding that the allegation has been established. Actual assigned investigation responsibilities and nonretaliation remain. Employees and third parties are strongly encouraged to use the policy’s reporting routes; the course does not give every learner the same supervisor duty or new investigative authority.

Personal support can remain specific. A person may want a naming request received without telling the room a history. That optional choice does not cancel Casey’s actual role. Conversely, Casey’s duty does not authorize broad circulation of the concern, a public personal account or an improvised official record change. Actual information and record requirements retain their appropriate arrangements. A course exercise cannot decide what real information is releasable or replace assigned responsibilities.

Actual daily equity work and qualifying prolonged or long-term actions scheduled for specified approvals retain the DHS Equity Policy’s toolkit and formal analysis or scan arrangements. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program and provides guidance, knowledge and feedback while staff do their equity work. Consultant support is not a universal checkpoint before an immediate required report. Privately explain Casey’s next step using the full example; no actual allegation or public confrontation is needed to learn the distinction.

items.title: Keep the conduct example and the report distinct
items.body: The policy’s name-conduct example retains its protected-class relationship and repeated or deliberate scope. Casey receives an allegation about that relationship, not a completed finding. The immediate report follows the specified supervisor role; it does not wait for Casey to settle the allegation independently.

items.title: Retain both support and duty
items.body: A particular support choice can remain optional while Casey follows actual procedures. Neither a declined biography nor an unaccepted apology cancels the report. This keeps the person’s naming request visible without making it a substitute for the assigned process.

items.title: Do not create unrelated authority
items.body: Receiving the concern does not permit publication, unrestricted record edits or an improvised investigation outside assigned procedures. Actual staff roles and information arrangements explain those decisions. The course can teach the distinction without awarding new authority through completion.

tabs.label: A naming lesson must prove the allegation first
tabs.body: Casey waits for a family history and a successful pronunciation test before reporting. Those conditions are not in the specified immediate supervisor duty. They would transfer the burden onto a personal performance while leaving the actual route unfulfilled.

tabs.label: An informal repair completes the process
tabs.body: Casey treats a proposed apology or changed greeting as a finding and closes the matter. The course supplies neither that authority nor an investigation result. A useful response may accompany the process while actual procedures and nonretaliation remain.

lessons.statement: Name the gain precisely and leave unconfirmed results open.

intro.heading: Keep a specific naming gain and its limits together
intro.body:
The example ends with one limited action. Ada revises the draft introduction to Mara Ellis and uses Jo in a private practice discussion. Mara replies, “That is the name I wanted in the introduction.” Jo says, “Jo works for this discussion.” These replies confirm the stated uses at that scope. The reading evening, public posting, spoken pronunciation, a record change and every future preference remain unconfirmed.

Ada can also describe a learning gain. She understands Mara’s recipe-card contribution recognition and Jo’s chosen stage-crew familiarity more clearly. These meanings widened the distance and seriousness judgments and changed her response. The gain does not require ranking the adults, assigning a developmental orientation or declaring that every person with a similar name or affiliation wants the same treatment. Another person’s meaning remains a question rather than a rule carried forward.

Mara’s reply should not become permission to retell the family story online. Jo’s reply should not become permission to shorten a different name or change an official record. The source guidance encouraged asking what a use needs; it did not make one response cover every purpose. Ada can retain the specific feedback and ask an appropriate later question if another use genuinely arises.

The separate workplace allegation remains with Casey’s actual responsibilities and assigned process. No performed report or investigation finding is supplied in that example. The learner can identify the required next step without recording it as completed. Neither the private naming action nor a course result fills that missing information. If the real situation differs, actual role and information arrangements guide the work rather than an invented universal schedule.

You can privately explain a naming expectation you understand differently, or continue only with the full example. A meaningful change in self-understanding is a valid outcome alongside a possible practical application. You do not need to stage a reading event, disclose a name history, collect another person’s voice or produce a work artifact. Participation is voluntary; Actual responsibilities remain.

A truthful closing account holds the particular action, the replies and the remaining questions together. It values what changed without promising permanent recognition, universal access, an approved event or resolution of a separate protected-class concern.

items.title: Receive the replies at their size
items.body: Mara confirms the requested introduction name and Jo confirms the current discussion address. These are useful specific replies, not permission for every publication or future context. Keeping their scope avoids losing a person’s choice while still recognizing that the proposed use was received.

items.title: Do not erase private understanding
items.body: Ada’s wider view has value even if no reading evening follows. The learned meanings can help her understand a former judgment without proving a public outcome. A learner can retain that insight privately, without turning another person’s account into a performance or a permanent cultural profile.

items.title: Keep different unknowns separate
items.body: Pronunciation, later use, actual record requirements and Casey’s process result need their own information. No missing reply is zero, refusal or a finding. A fitting continuation follows the particular question and actual arrangements rather than an unlimited new disclosure exercise.

tabs.label: Specific acknowledgment becomes every permission
tabs.body: Ada calls Mara’s reply approval for the family story, event, recording and official records. The words confirm the introduction name, not those different uses. The acknowledgment can be valuable while those questions remain unanswered.

tabs.label: No public event means no learning
tabs.body: Ada discards the replies and wider interpretation because the evening has not occurred. That erases supplied actions and intrinsic understanding. Practical later results are separate from the specific gain already described in the example.

tabs.label: The gain and the open questions remain together
tabs.body: Ada retains the revised draft, current discussion address and specific replies, alongside the learned recognition and familiarity meanings. Another use still needs its relevant question and actual arrangements. This closes the learning honestly without a public proof requirement or a personal rank.

remember: Participation in this learning is voluntary.

sections.heading: Receive the request and purpose
items: Mara offers Mara Ellis for the introduction. Jo offers Jo for discussion. Neither establishes a formal record, nationality, legal status, relationship or language qualification.
W3C’s general international-name guidance prompts questions about purpose and assumptions; it is not a universal perfect form or authority to revise actual agency records.

sections.heading: Ask only what the use needs
items: Ada’s proposed questions distinguish an introduction name and a discussion address. A required family story would change the purpose into cultural disclosure.

Public posting, recordings and official corrections have their own requirements and assigned arrangements. An introduction answer does not authorize every later use or decide information classification.

sections.heading: Let particular meaning widen a judgment
items: Mara learned contribution recognition through named recipe cards. Jo learned chosen familiarity through asking for a stage-crew address. These meanings widen Ada’s distance and seriousness labels.

A proposed response receives Mara Ellis for the introduction and Jo for discussion without creating a group script or ranking name lengths. It does not establish permission to retell their stories. Private self-understanding can matter without an event.

sections.heading: Receive a correction proportionately
items: Mara asks for both words when her contribution is introduced. Acknowledge that request and invite a relevant pronunciation clarification without a compulsory biography or unlimited public teaching.

A written correction does not supply pronunciation, recording permission, every future preference or an official record change. Good intent does not erase the specific request; the person need not reassure the speaker before it is received.

sections.heading: Keep actual roles intact
items: Supervisor Casey receives a protected-class naming allegation. Managers and supervisors immediately report all protected-class allegations or incidents to HR or agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow actual complaint/investigation procedures and/or the Affirmative Action Plan. Cultural proof, an apology, course terminology or consultant approval cannot delay that duty.

The policy’s repeated or deliberate name-conduct example retains its protected-class relationship; an allegation report is not a finding. Employees and third parties have strongly encouraged reporting routes, not identical supervisor duties assigned by the course. Actual information, records, assigned investigation and nonretaliation remain.

DHS daily equity and qualifying prolonged or long-term actions scheduled for specified approvals retain their relevant toolkit/formal analysis or scan and permitted customized arrangements. Staff do their equity work with Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant program guidance and leadership, without a new universal gate. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.

sections.heading: Describe the gain honestly
items: Ada changes the draft and private discussion use. Mara confirms the introduction name and Jo confirms this discussion address. The meanings widen Ada’s view, while public posting, pronunciation, official records and the separate process outcome remain open.

No missing result becomes refusal or zero, and no specific acknowledgment becomes every permission. Continue privately or through a chosen actual task’s arrangements without a public proof requirement or permanent personal score.
